evidence.excerpt: This book will help you find the weak part instead of blaming “AI” as though it were one indivisible object. Read the chapters in order to build the complete picture. Use the separate Concept Index when you need to look up one term—such as token, context, memory, routing or agent—and then jump to the chapter where that term does real work.

This is the first lesson of the whole book: the quality of an AI result depends on more than the wording of one prompt. It depends on what the system is trying to help you do, what information reached it, what operations ran, what the model produced and what you checked before acting.

Later chapters will open each part carefully: how models are trained and run; how tokens and context windows affect what fits; how session and memory differ; what retrieval, tools, permissions, routing and wrappers add; how agents and multi-step loops work; and why convincing answers can still fail. The Concept Index will let you find any one term without turning the book itself into a dictionary.

You did not consult one all-knowing thing. You used an **AI system**: the whole working arrangement that received your request and produced the result. That arrangement includes the product you opened, the instructions and material available for this task, at least one trained model, and the software that presents the answer. Some systems can also search, calculate, retrieve documents or take actions. The exact arrangement varies from product to product.

The **model** is an important part of that system, but it is not the whole system. It is the trained component that processes input and produces an output. The product and surrounding software shape what reaches it, which other capabilities are available and what you eventually see.
We will begin with one decision and follow it all the way through. Nothing floats around as a loose definition. Every part earns its name by changing what happens next.

Not every AI product has the same tools, and not every available tool runs on every request. The useful question is not “Does this AI have tools?” It is “What operation actually ran for this answer, and can I inspect what came back?”

1. **What decision am I actually trying to make?** If the system solved a narrower problem, restate the real one.
2. **What information did this answer actually use?** Check the messages, files, dates and missing facts that mattered.
3. **What current source or operation supports the consequential claims?** Inspect the returned evidence; do not treat fluency as a citation.

aiEditorialAnalysis.prompt: Why can the Census finding that 30% of men but 17% of women use AI daily at work not be read as evidence that women are less able or less interested in AI?
aiEditorialAnalysis.response: Because how often someone uses AI depends heavily on conditions her employer controls: whether she was given an approved tool, paid time to learn it, and an invitation to a project where it is used. Two equally interested colleagues with different conditions will show different usage. On top of that, if managers pick trial teams only from existing users, early access differences compound, so a frequency gap can grow without any difference in ability. The survey also only measures self-reported frequency among people who already used AI — it never measured skill, interest or access at all.
aiEditorialAnalysis.expectedEvidence: An accurate answer should cite the conditions mechanism (tool, paid time, invitation) from P006, the compounding selection effect from P007, and the measurement limits from P003–P004 (different populations; frequency is not ability).
aiEditorialAnalysis.assessment: The article fully supports this answer: P006 supplies the conditions mechanism with an explicit epistemic boundary, P007 supplies the compounding step, and P004 supplies the measurement limits, all in ordinary language.

aiEditorialAnalysis.prompt: Using the article's mechanism, what should the director check before treating the login gap as a preference or ability gap, and how should the committee be selected?
aiEditorialAnalysis.response: First check the conditions: night nurses may have had no scheduled paid time to learn the tool, restricted terminals, or no invitation to the pilot — so their lower logins may reflect access, not interest. Second, avoid the compounding step: selecting the committee only from heavy users would hand a further opportunity to whoever had early access, entrenching the gap. Instead, publish visible selection criteria, include a supported route for non-users (training time within their shift workload), and judge success by useful work and sound judgment rather than a daily-usage target.

candidateEvidence.excerpt: Women accounted for 26% of U.S. hires into AI occupations in 2025, compared with 50% of hires into other occupations, according to research LinkedIn published on August 18. Its separate international leadership analysis found that women held 13% of top executive AI leadership roles at AI companies. These figures describe who is getting hired and who holds authority.

Those are different groups and different questions. The hiring figures do not cover every job in which someone uses AI. The frequency figures do not measure skill, interest or whether daily use would help someone do her job. Neither report establishes why a particular woman has less access to an opportunity.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: They accounted for just 26% of U.S. AI hires in 2025, compared with 50% of hires into non-AI occupations. The gap grows at the top: across 27 countries, women hold only 13% of C-suite AI leadership roles at AI companies.

claimMap.scopeAndFreshness: P002 matches the LinkedIn passage exactly: 26% of U.S. AI hires in 2025 vs 50% for non-AI occupations, and 13% of C-suite/top executive AI leadership roles at AI companies; attribution and the August 18 date are retained, and the article correctly notes these are separate analyses describing representation, not ability.

candidateEvidence.excerpt: A U.S. Census Bureau report published on August 11 measures something different: how often people use AI at work. Among workers who had used AI for at least one of the tasks surveyed, 30% of men and 17% of women reported using it every day in the previous week. The survey was conducted in March 2026.

Those are different groups and different questions. The hiring figures do not cover every job in which someone uses AI. The frequency figures do not measure skill, interest or whether daily use would help someone do her job. Neither report establishes why a particular woman has less access to an opportunity.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: When AI users at work were asked how much they used AI in the last week, 30% of male workers said they used it every day, compared with 17% of female workers. Half of female workers said they used it at least one day, but not every day, and 41% of male workers said the same.

About 55% of U.S. workers said they have used Artificial Intelligence (AI) on the job for at least one of 11 tasks asked about on the U.S. Census Bureau’s March 2026 Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS).

claimMap.scopeAndFreshness: P003 matches the Census passage: among AI users at work, 30% of men vs 17% of women reported daily use in the previous week, from the March 2026 survey published August 11; the article preserves the source's limits by stating frequency does not measure skill, interest or causes (P004).
